beats.text: One sociologist kept some 90,000 index cards.
beats.note: Niklas Luhmann built it up from 1952 to 1953 onwards.

beats.text: He never ordered cards by topic.
beats.note: Each slip got a number and kept it for ever. A slip numbered 57/12 could be continued by 57/13, and an insertion became 57/12a.

beats.text: He did not invent the card box.
beats.note: In the 16th century Conrad Gessner devised a method where notes could be rearranged at any time, and suggested gluing slips onto sheets.

beats.text: He called the box a partner in communication.
beats.note: After more than twenty-six years he wrote that the approach was viable. He described the result as an alter ego you can talk to.

beats.text: The cards were digitised and put online.
beats.note: Bielefeld University made them available in 2019.

beats.text: The system worked because every note had a fixed address.

beats.line: Number your notes and never move them.
